frameworks.name: Fix Back to Front
frameworks.definition: Sequence business improvements from offer (what you sell) to sales process (how you sell) to targeting (who to sell to) to traffic (how they find you); always repair downstream before upstream.

frameworks.name: Seed of Doubt Framework
frameworks.definition: When selling against commodity competitors on price, enumerate risk, speed, and ease dimensions the competitor fails on; surfacing these variables in a sales call shifts the buyer's comparison frame from price to value.

frameworks.name: VIP + Standard Tier Architecture
frameworks.definition: Lead every sales conversation at the premium tier (VIP); move prospects down to standard only when they self-identify as budget-constrained, preserving margin from high-willingness-to-pay buyers while retaining volume.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when a service business charges by the hour with no differentiation, it becomes a commodity and customers will always choose the cheapest hourly rate, regardless of quality. The only way to escape the hourly price race is to break the comparison frame by quoting by job or by value-bundled package rather than by unit of time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: When two offers share the same measurement unit (e.g., $/hour), buyers strip out all other variables and compare only that unit. Switching to a job-based or value-bundled price removes the direct comparison axis.
bounded_by: Does not apply to regulated billing contexts where hourly rates are legally required

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that realtor-sourced moving jobs at Flixly Moving generate roughly 3x revenue per job compared to Google Maps or SEO-sourced jobs ($3,000+ per realtor job vs. ~$1,000 per Google job in the same month), because realtors refer clients who are in the middle of a home sale and therefore have more money and less price sensitivity than average residential movers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Realtors refer clients who recently completed a home transaction and are therefore in a higher-income segment with less price sensitivity than renters or budget movers.

numbers.axis: revenue per job by acquisition channel

bounded_by: Single-month sample from one small market; may not hold in lower-income markets or with unscreened realtors

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that offering a channel partner (realtor) a free VIP service upgrade for every client they refer is more compelling than offering the partner a cash referral fee ($250), because the upgrade makes the realtor look like they have exclusive access for their clients rather than appearing to take a kickback.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service businesses where trust and reputation are the agent's primary asset
claims.mechanism: Realtors earn their fee by demonstrating expertise and exclusive relationships; a VIP upgrade reinforces this positioning for them, whereas a cash incentive can signal misaligned incentives to their client.
bounded_by: May not apply to purely transactional referral relationships where cash is explicitly requested

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that service businesses targeting channel partners (realtors) should pitch the brokerage principal rather than individual agents, because one brokerage principal can commit 5-20 agents whose combined deal flow may produce roughly 5 houses per month per brokerage, stacking each week a new brokerage is signed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A brokerage principal controls all agents' referral behavior; one agreement replaces 5-20 individual negotiations and creates an ongoing recurring deal flow rather than one-off referrals.

numbers.axis: monthly deal flow per brokerage partnership

bounded_by: Assumes brokerage principal enforces the referral agreement; depends on relationship quality with principal

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that if a customer calls only asking about price and has no other variables to consider, price will always be the deciding factor. The purpose of a well-structured sales process is to introduce additional variables (risk, speed, ease) so the comparison shifts from a single-axis price check to a multi-axis value assessment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: inbound or outbound sales call for a service business
buyer is price-comparing between similar-looking options
claims.mechanism: When only one variable (price) is salient, the buyer must select on price. Surfacing additional variables (quality certifications, insurance, included materials, price cap) forces a multi-dimensional comparison where the higher-priced option can win on net value.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that in any service sales context, a sales rep should always lead with the premium (VIP) tier rather than standard, because buyers with money will simply say yes without resistance, and budget-constrained buyers will self-select down to the lower tier - meaning starting at standard leaves money on the table from high-willingness-to-pay customers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business with at least two defined offer tiers
claims.mechanism: Affluent buyers have already decided to spend; starting at premium captures their willingness to pay. Budget buyers will volunteer their constraint, triggering the tier step-down naturally with no loss.
bounded_by: Does not apply in fixed-price or transparent-pricing contexts (e.g., e-commerce, self-serve SaaS)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi advises that in service businesses where quality can vary at the worker level, creating an internal certification or tier system (e.g., Level 1 / Level 2 / Level 3 Master Mover) provides a credible differentiation layer even when the internal standard is self-defined, because buyers perceive labeled tiers as meaningful proof of quality and it sows doubt about uncertified competitors.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: commodity market where competitors use undifferentiated staff
claims.mechanism: Buyers cannot directly observe worker quality; a named tier with a stated threshold (e.g., 50+ completed moves) functions as a credible proxy for quality and creates a comparison disadvantage for competitors who make no such claim.
bounded_by: Requires the business to actually enforce the stated threshold to avoid reputation risk

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that charging a same-day premium (starting at 10%, targeting 20%) for last-minute or emergency service requests is justified because speed is one of the highest-value attributes customers will pay for, and failing to capture this premium leaves pure margin on the table since no additional cost is incurred.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Customers booking same-day face no alternatives; their willingness to pay is maximal at this moment. The business incurs zero additional cost but captures urgency premium.

numbers.axis: same-day surcharge as % of base price

bounded_by: Applies only when availability is genuine; manufacturing false urgency destroys trust

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for commodity service businesses, adding a price cap (a stated maximum the customer will not be charged beyond a quoted estimate) is a powerful sales tool because most competitors do not offer one, so asking 'did the other guys give you a cap?' in a sales call immediately highlights that competitors have open-ended billing exposure.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: customer is comparing multiple providers by price
claims.mechanism: Unlimited hourly billing is a hidden risk most buyers have not thought about until asked. The cap removes the risk dimension from the competitor's apparently lower hourly rate, making the higher-priced capped provider a safer choice on expected total cost.
bounded_by: Requires business to maintain a buffer in estimate to avoid taking losses; Hormozi suggested a 50% buffer over expected estimate

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that using AI to personalize the first outbound SMS message to each prospect in a large list (feeding the list into an AI agent that researches each person and generates a custom opener) will outperform sending a generic template to the same list, and will also reduce spam filtering by SMS carriers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: SMS outreach to a list of 1,000+ prospects
B2C or B2B service business with identifiable prospect profiles
claims.mechanism: SMS carriers flag numbers that send identical messages to hundreds of recipients; varied personalized messages bypass this detection. Personalization also increases open and response rates by demonstrating relevance.
bounded_by: Requires AI output review before sending to catch hallucinated or inappropriate personalization

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that when a foreman (not the owner) asks for a five-star review on behalf of the crew and mentions that movers get a performance spiff from ownership for five-star reviews, the likelihood of a customer actually leaving a review increases substantially compared to an owner asking directly.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: on-site service business with on-the-ground crew
review request at moment of job completion
claims.mechanism: The foreman asking on behalf of the crew creates a social appeal (helping a worker) rather than a business appeal (helping the owner). Customers are more likely to act for individuals than corporations, especially when they witnessed the labor directly.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that service businesses selling to the bottom of the market (renters, budget movers) face structurally lower revenue per transaction and lower margins than those serving wealthy buyers (home sellers, estate movers), and that the realtor channel provides an early signal for the wealthier avatar the business should migrate toward.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: choosing between renter/budget segment vs. home-sale segment
claims.mechanism: Wealthier buyers evaluate moving cost as a small fraction of a large transaction (home sale); they optimize for certainty and service quality rather than hourly rate, enabling higher margin captures.
bounded_by: Requires business to develop premium offer credibility before migrating avatar

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that posting a consistent format of before-and-after content (house full before move, house empty after, then destination house empty before, destination full after) combined with a five-star review at the end of each clip creates a compound proof loop that builds organic social credibility and supports brokerage-level sales conversations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The before-after format provides inherent narrative closure and visual proof of outcome; stacking this with a customer review reduces the cognitive distance between 'they did a good job here' and 'I should hire them.' Repeated posting compounds the social signal over time.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi identifies three dimensions along which a service business can build differentiation against commodity competitors: risk (e.g., background-checked vs. unvetted labor, insurance coverage), speed (e.g., same-day availability), and ease (e.g., materials included, no hidden fees, price cap). Each dimension, when named in a sales conversation, shifts the frame from price comparison to value comparison.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: labor-based service business competing primarily on price
bounded_by: Dimensions must be genuinely delivered, not just claimed; false claims destroy reviews and referrals

claims.text: Alex Hormozi diagnoses that a business losing deals primarily on price is not experiencing a lead-generation problem but a sales process problem, because the prospect already found the business and engaged; the cause of loss is an inability to differentiate value during the sales conversation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: inbound lead flow is already present
primary stated reason for loss is price
bounded_by: If total lead volume is genuinely too low to generate enough closed deals even at 100% close rate, this is a lead volume problem, not a sales process problem

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that a business at the nail-it phase (finding product-market fit, establishing differentiated offer, building first team) must stabilize and differentiate the model before scaling to multiple locations, because scaling a commodity model only compounds the race-to-the-bottom pricing problem at each new location.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service business with fewer than 10 employees

examples.text: During the coaching session, Hormozi walked through how Nas (Flixly Moving) should restructure a sales call. Instead of immediately quoting an hourly rate, the rep would ask qualifying questions: How many rooms? Do you care about the qualifications of the movers? Do you have packing materials? Do you have items valued over $500 (triggering an insurance conversation)? Is this today (triggering same-day premium)? After gathering this information, the rep presents the VIP offer (master movers + materials + insurance) at $195/hour and only steps down to standard ($165/hour) if the buyer self-identifies as budget-constrained. This structure means the buyer has considered risk, ease, and speed before they ever compare on price.

Hormozi described his experience at his gym business where he created three levels of internal trainer certification (Level 1, Level 2, Level 3 Master Trainer). The thresholds were self-defined: Level 3 required completing 1,000 client sessions. Customers consistently reacted with positive surprise at the 'Level 3 Master Trainer' label even though the certification was internal. Hormozi applied this directly to the moving context, suggesting Flixly designate movers as Level 3 once they had completed 50-100 moves, and position VIP moves as exclusively staffed by Level 3 master movers.

Hormozi illustrated how to sell the price cap in a sales call: the rep asks the prospect if the competing company offered a price cap. When the prospect says no, the rep explains that an hourly rate with no cap means the movers could take 20 hours to complete a 4-hour move with no recourse for the buyer. This surfaces an invisible risk the buyer had not considered, making the slightly higher all-in quote with a cap feel like the safer and potentially cheaper option on an expected-value basis.

Hormozi proposed that Flixly offer all agents at a target brokerage free VIP upgrades for any client move as the opener for a brokerage-level deal. Once one agent already has a good experience, Nas should show up in person to that brokerage office with donuts, meet all the agents, and present the upgrade offer to the principal. The in-person visit converts a single agent relationship into a brokerage-wide relationship, multiplying deal flow from one referral source into potentially 20 agents each sending deals.

Hormozi noted that when Nas mentioned his wife quit her six-figure job to support the business, his moving costs Alex moved were approximately $25,000 - a sum he did not even remember precisely because he was optimizing for completion certainty rather than hourly rate. He used this to illustrate that wealthy buyers (in his case, a homeowner moving an entire house) have a completely different decision frame than renters: they want a guaranteed outcome and will pay substantially more for it without negotiating on price.

practices.text: When closing the review request at job completion, have the foreman (not the owner) ask the customer: 'Was this a good experience? The guys get a small spiff from ownership for five-star reviews - it would really mean a lot to them.' Follow with a link.

Post a before-and-after social clip at every job site: film the origin house full, film origin house empty, film destination empty, film destination full, end with the five-star review text on screen.

Feed a large prospect list into an AI agent to research each person online and generate a personalized SMS opener; review the outputs quickly for quality, then send - the personalization reduces spam filtering and increases response rate compared to a generic template.

When an individual realtor responds positively, visit their brokerage office in person with donuts; offer every agent a free VIP upgrade for any client move in exchange for being the brokerage's default moving company.
Continuously raise the VIP tier price until buyers say no; always maintain the standard tier as the fallback so the business does not lose volume while testing the price ceiling.

In a sales call for a labor service, ask explicitly: 'Do you care about the qualifications of the movers?' Many customers have not thought about whether movers are background-checked or experienced; the question itself creates a preference the business can then satisfy.
